en: To make something impure or weaker by adding a cheaper or harmful substance
hook: ADULTERATE: an ADULT trick to cheat by mixing in cheap stuff.
story: Adulterate. For months, the families on Lamia's street complained that their milk tasted thin and watery. Nobody could prove anything. Then, one foggy morning, Lamia's grandmother woke early and caught the milkman behind the mosque, pouring tap water into his cans before delivery. He had been adulterating the milk to stretch his profits. To adulterate is to spoil something's purity by mixing in a cheaper or harmful substance, like water in milk or chalk in medicine.

gre.s: Inspectors discovered that the supplier had found a way to ____ the saffron with dyed corn silk, passing off the cheap filler as the costly spice.
gre.clue: passing off the cheap filler as the costly spice

example: Food inspectors in Dhaka fined several shops for adulterating turmeric powder with brick dust to increase its weight.

en: To increase the power, wealth, or importance of; to make something seem greater than it is
bn: ক্ষমতা বা মর্যাদা বাড়ানো; বাড়িয়ে দেখানো
hook: AG-GRAND-ize: to make yourself GRAND.
story: Aggrandize. When the new mayor took office, strange things began to happen. A giant statue of him appeared at the town gate. Three roads were renamed after his family. His face smiled from every billboard, beside words like Visionary and Father of Progress. He had built almost nothing, yet he looked larger every day. To aggrandize is to increase power, wealth, or importance, or to make something seem greater than it is. Self-aggrandizing people constantly enlarge their own image.

gre.s: Rather than ____ his own role, the modest scientist repeatedly credited his students for the discovery.
gre.clue: the modest scientist repeatedly credited his students

example: The dictator's statues and portraits were designed to aggrandize a man who had never actually fought in a single battle.

en: To grow, spread, or multiply quickly
hook: BURGEON: a BURGER shop that grows into a giant chain overnight.
story: Burgeon. Ten years ago, Farhan's cousin started a tiny online shop selling handmade notebooks from her bedroom. She shipped five orders a week. Then social media found her. Fifty orders a week. Five hundred. Today she runs a warehouse with forty employees. Her business burgeoned: it grew and flourished rapidly, like buds bursting open in spring. Burgeoning populations, burgeoning cities, burgeoning careers. Think of a tiny burger stall that suddenly becomes a nationwide chain.

gre.s: Scientists warn that, unless strict controls are introduced, the city's population will continue to ____, straining already overloaded water supplies.
gre.clue: straining already overloaded water supplies

example: Online clothing shops have burgeoned across Bangladesh, with thousands of small sellers now taking orders through social media.

en: Cautious and wary; reluctant to give or risk
hook: CHARY: CAREFUL and wARY.
story: Chary. Tanvir once lent his notes to a classmate, who copied them, submitted them as his own, and got Tanvir accused of plagiarism. Since then, Tanvir is chary of lending anything. He asks questions, hesitates, and usually says no. He is chary: cautious and wary, reluctant to give or risk. Chary is related to care, so a chary person is careful. Being chary of praise means giving it rarely. Synonyms: wary, cautious, leery.

gre.s: Having lost heavily in the last market crash, investors were understandably ____ of new technology stocks, refusing to commit money without years of proven profits.
gre.clue: refusing to commit money without years of proven profits

example: After being cheated once by a fake recruiting agency, Kamal was chary of any job offer that asked for money in advance.

en: To restrict within limits; to draw a line around
hook: CIRCUM-SCRIBE: draw (scribe) a CIRCLE around it.
story: Circumscribe. Lamia's grandmother was a brilliant student in the 1960s, top of her school in mathematics. But her choices were circumscribed by tradition: which subjects she could study, whether she could attend university, and whom she would marry were all decided for her. Her world was drawn inside a small circle. To circumscribe is to restrict within limits. Circum means around, scribe means draw. In geometry, you circumscribe a circle around a shape.

gre.s: The new law sought to ____ the president's powers, limiting his ability to declare emergencies without parliamentary approval.
gre.clue: limiting his ability to declare emergencies

example: Her illness circumscribed her travels, but from her balcony in Old Dhaka she wrote vivid stories about the whole country.

en: An unexpected, embarrassing mishap or minor dispute
hook: CONTRE-TEMPS: French for 'against time' — bad timing.
story: Contretemps. At Joya's engagement ceremony, the groom's mother arrived wearing exactly the same sari as the bride's mother. There was an awkward silence, a few stiff smiles, and then a short argument about who should change. The family still laughs about that contretemps: an unexpected, embarrassing mishap or minor dispute. The word is French, meaning against the time, and is pronounced KON-truh-tahn. Synonyms: mishap, hitch, squabble.

gre.s: The diplomats' brief ____ over seating arrangements, though embarrassing at the time, was soon forgotten amid the far weightier negotiations that followed.
gre.clue: soon forgotten amid the far weightier negotiations

example: A minor contretemps over who would cut the wedding cake briefly soured the mood between the two families.

en: To capture someone's complete attention; to fascinate
hook: ENTHRALL: like a THRALL (slave) to the story.
story: Enthrall. Every evening, Grandfather Moti sits on the veranda and tells ghost stories about the old banyan tree. All the children of the neighbourhood gather at his feet. Nobody fidgets, nobody checks a phone; even the cat seems to listen. He enthralls them: he captures their complete attention and fascinates them. A thrall was once a slave, so an enthralled audience is held captive by wonder. Synonyms: captivate, spellbind, mesmerize, rivet. Opposite: bore.

gre.s: Her storytelling could ____ even the most restless audience: children who usually fidgeted through lessons sat motionless until the final word.
gre.clue: children who usually fidgeted through lessons sat motionless until the final word

example: The documentary on deep-sea creatures enthralled my younger brother, who watched it four times in a single weekend.

en: To give unclear answers on purpose so as not to take a stand
hook: EQUI-VOCATE: EQUAL VOICES, saying both yes and no at once.
story: Equivocate. A reporter asked the minister a simple question: "Will fuel prices rise next month?" The minister smiled. "Well, many complex factors are involved. We are carefully monitoring global trends. Of course, the people's welfare is our highest priority." He spoke for three minutes and said nothing at all. He equivocated: used vague, ambiguous language to avoid committing to an answer. Equi means equal, vocate means voice: speaking equally for yes and no at once.

gre.s: Pressed to say whether she supported the bill, the candidate continued to ____, offering answers so qualified that both sides claimed her as an ally.
gre.clue: offering answers so qualified that both sides claimed her

example: When the journalist asked whether layoffs were planned, the company spokesman equivocated, saying only that all options were being studied.

en: To attack someone or something with fierce criticism
hook: EX-CORIATE: to strip off the skin (corium), with harsh words.
story: Excoriate. A new bridge in a northern town cracked only six months after it opened. At the public hearing, an engineer stood up and tore the construction company apart: cheap steel, stolen funds, ignored warnings, and lies to the press. For an hour he spared nothing. He excoriated the company: he criticized it very severely. Literally, excoriate means to strip off the skin, from the Latin corium, meaning hide. Such criticism feels like being skinned. Synonyms: lambaste, castigate, berate.

gre.s: Reviewers did not merely criticize the novel; they chose to ____ it, condemning its plot, its prose, and its author's integrity in the harshest possible terms.
gre.clue: in the harshest possible terms

example: In a fiery editorial, the newspaper excoriated the factory owners who had locked the fire exits.

en: To show or declare that someone is not guilty
hook: EX-CULPA: out of (ex) guilt (culpa, culprit).
story: Exculpate. For two years, everyone in the office believed that Babu, the quiet security guard, had stolen the money from the safe. He lost his job, and neighbours whispered about him. Then an IT technician recovered deleted CCTV footage. It showed the real thief: a senior manager. Babu was exculpated: officially cleared of blame. Ex means out of, culpa means guilt, as in culprit. Exculpate is the opposite of inculpate, which means to accuse.

gre.s: The newly discovered letters seemed to ____ the accused general, showing that he had opposed the massacre rather than ordered it.
gre.clue: showing that he had opposed the massacre rather than ordered it

example: DNA tests finally exculpated the farmer, who had spent eleven years in prison for a murder he did not commit.

en: Inclined to cause disagreement and division into factions
hook: FACTIOUS: creating FACTIONS.
story: Factious. The university debating club once had forty happy members. Then two senior students began fighting over who would lead it. Each recruited loyal followers, spread rumours about the other, and blocked every proposal from the rival camp. By the end of the year, the club had split into two angry groups. Their factious behavior had divided everyone. Factious means inclined to cause disagreement and division into factions. Do not confuse it with fractious, meaning unruly, or factitious, meaning artificial. Synonyms: divisive, partisan.

gre.s: The once unified party had grown so ____ that its members spent more energy attacking rival wings than opposing the government.
gre.clue: spent more energy attacking rival wings than opposing the government

example: The factious student union split into three groups that could not agree even on the date of the annual festival.

en: To deny or contradict
hook: GAINSAY: to say AGAINST.
story: Gainsay. The evidence against the thief was overwhelming: CCTV footage, his fingerprints on the safe, and three witnesses who saw him running away. His lawyer stood up, opened her mouth, then closed it again. Nobody could gainsay the facts. To gainsay is to deny or contradict something. It is usually used with a negative: "There is no gainsaying her talent" means her talent is undeniable. Think: to say against.

gre.s: No one could ____ the champion's skill; even her fiercest critics admitted that she was the finest player of her generation.
gre.clue: even her fiercest critics admitted

example: There is no gainsaying the importance of the garment sector, which employs millions of workers across Bangladesh.

en: Not fitting the rules of polite, proper behavior
hook: IN-DECOROUS: NOT showing DECORUM.
story: Indecorous. At a solemn funeral gathering in his village, Babu's phone suddenly rang with a loud dance song. Worse, he answered it and began laughing about a cricket score while the imam was still praying. The elders glared at him. His behavior was indecorous: not in keeping with good taste and the propriety the occasion demanded. Decorum means proper, dignified behavior, so indecorous is its opposite. It is milder than indecent; it means improper, not obscene. Synonyms: unseemly, improper, unbecoming.

gre.s: Many guests found the best man's crude jokes at the memorial service ____, since such levity seemed out of place at so solemn an occasion.
gre.clue: seemed out of place at so solemn an occasion

example: Several members of parliament considered it indecorous for a minister to dance on stage at a campaign rally.

en: Unable to be avoided; inevitable
hook: IN-E-LUCTABLE: you can't struggle (luctari) out of it.
story: Ineluctable. Imran tried everything to avoid the final calculus exam. He hoped for a strike, a flood, even a cyclone. None came. The exam date arrived, as exam dates always do. Some things are ineluctable: impossible to avoid; inevitable. Ageing, death, and deadlines are ineluctable. The word comes from the Latin luctari, to wrestle or struggle; something ineluctable is a thing you cannot wrestle your way out of. Synonyms: inevitable, inescapable, unavoidable.

gre.s: Many historians once believed the empire's decline was ____, the result of forces no ruler could have resisted; newer scholarship stresses specific mistakes that might easily have been avoided.
gre.clue: forces no ruler could have resisted

example: Rising sea levels make the ineluctable retreat of some coastal villages a matter of planning rather than debate.

en: To persuade someone by flattery or deception
hook: INVEIGLE: like a VEIL over the truth to lure someone in.
story: Inveigle. A smooth-talking salesman visited Rahim's grandfather in Cumilla. He praised the old man's wisdom, admired his garden, called him uncle, and touched his feet. Within an hour, he had talked him into signing up for an expensive insurance plan he did not need. The salesman had inveigled him: persuaded him by flattery or deception. Hear the word as in-vague-le: luring someone in with vague, sweet talk. Synonyms: cajole, wheedle, entice, beguile.

gre.s: Through a combination of flattery and false promises, the con artist managed to ____ several elderly investors into handing over their life savings.
gre.clue: Through a combination of flattery and false promises

example: With flattering letters and fake awards, a bogus publisher inveigled dozens of first-time poets in Khulna into paying for worthless print runs.

en: To scold or criticize someone fiercely
hook: LAMBASTE: LAMB gets BASTED (beaten) with harsh words.
story: Lambaste. Arif's team submitted a careless project report, full of copied paragraphs and wrong numbers. In the next meeting, the department head lambasted them in front of everyone. She listed every error, called the work disgraceful, and demanded a full rewrite by Monday. To lambaste is to criticize harshly. The word joins two old verbs that both meant to beat, lam and baste. It is close to excoriate. Synonyms: berate, castigate, slam.

gre.s: Rather than praising the minister's long-delayed reforms, opposition leaders chose to ____ them as too little, too late, and a betrayal of earlier promises.
gre.clue: too little, too late, and a betrayal of earlier promises

example: Food bloggers lambasted the new restaurant on Gulshan Avenue for serving cold biryani at outrageous prices.

en: A heavy tiredness that drains body or mind of energy
hook: LASSITUDE: a LAZY attitude.
story: Lassitude. After three weeks of typhoid, Nadia was finally free of fever, yet she could barely lift her head from the pillow. Books lay unopened; even talking on the phone felt like hard work. The doctor said this lassitude was normal after a long illness: a heavy weariness and lack of energy, of body or mind. Lassitude sounds like lazy attitude, but it is closer to exhaustion than laziness. Dhaka's humid June heat brings lassitude too. Synonyms: lethargy, languor, fatigue.

gre.s: The sweltering afternoon induced a general ____ among the delegates; several dozed in their seats, and no one had the energy to challenge the chairman's proposals.
gre.clue: no one had the energy to challenge the chairman's proposals

example: Weeks of dengue fever left Rumana in a lassitude so deep that she could barely climb the stairs to her flat.

en: To make a great public fuss over someone
bn: বীরের মতো সম্মান করা; তারকা বানিয়ে দেওয়া
hook: LIONIZE: treated like the LION, king of the jungle.
story: Lionize. A shy girl from a fishing village in Bhola won the international mathematics olympiad. Within a week she was everywhere: TV interviews, newspaper covers, reception ceremonies, a meeting with the prime minister. People asked for her autograph in the street. She was lionized: treated as a celebrity and hero. Picture being treated like the lion, king of the jungle. Societies often lionize their heroes, though sometimes the wrong ones.

gre.s: Although the press rushed to ____ the scientist after her discovery, she found the constant attention exhausting and retreated from public life.
gre.clue: she found the constant attention exhausting

example: When the young mountaineer returned from Everest, newspapers lionized her and schools invited her to speak every week.

en: Noisy and difficult to control
hook: OBSTREPEROUS: makes an OBSTACLE with noise.
story: Obstreperous. The night train from Dhaka to Chittagong was quiet until six young men boarded. They shouted, banged on the windows, played music at full volume, and argued with the ticket checker who asked them to sit down. When he threatened to call the police, they only shouted louder. The other passengers sighed at the obstreperous group: noisy and difficult to control. The word comes from Latin for making a racket, and it even sounds loud and clumsy. Synonyms: unruly, boisterous, rowdy.

gre.s: The substitute teacher could not control the ____ students, who shouted over one another, ignored her instructions, and refused to stay in their seats.
gre.clue: shouted over one another, ignored her instructions

example: The flight attendants had to calm an obstreperous passenger who kept shouting about the delay and pounding the seat.

en: Transparently clear; easily understood
hook: PELLUCID: like LUCID, light shines through.
story: Pellucid. Professor Haque's explanation of probability was so pellucid that even students who had failed math three times understood every step. He used coins, cricket, and rain forecasts, no jargon at all. Afterward, a student said it felt like a window had been cleaned. The lake at Nilgiri was pellucid too, clear right to the bottom. Pellucid means transparently clear, in water or in writing. Synonyms: lucid, limpid.

gre.s: The textbook's ____ explanations, free of jargon and full of simple examples, made a notoriously difficult subject accessible to beginners.
gre.clue: free of jargon and full of simple examples

example: The physicist's pellucid lecture on black holes left even the history students in the audience nodding along.

en: Quick to notice and understand what others miss
hook: PERSPICACIOUS: PERCEPTIVE, sees through everything.
story: Perspicacious. Everyone in the office thought the new accountant was perfect: polite, hardworking, always early. Only Rumana noticed that he stayed late on exactly the days when money went missing, and that his expensive watch did not match his salary. Her hunch led to an audit, and the fraud was exposed. She was perspicacious: having keen insight and understanding. It shares a root with perspective, seeing through. Do not confuse it with perspicuous, meaning clearly expressed. Synonyms: perceptive, astute, shrewd.

gre.s: A ____ observer of political trends, she foresaw the government's collapse months before other analysts noticed even the first signs of trouble.
gre.clue: foresaw the government's collapse months before other analysts

example: A perspicacious bank teller noticed that the signature on the cheque was slightly off and quietly called the manager.

en: To be an early sign or representation of something later
hook: PRE-FIGURE: a FIGURE of what's coming BEFORE it arrives.
story: Prefigure. At age eight, Anika took apart the family radio and rebuilt it, with only one screw left over. At twelve, she wired a doorbell for the neighbours. Today she is an electrical engineer. Her childhood tinkering prefigured her career: it was an early sign of what would come later. Pre means before, and figure means shape: a shape that appears before the real thing. A writer's early stories may prefigure her mature themes. Synonyms: foreshadow, anticipate.

gre.s: The architect's student sketches, with their sweeping curves and conspicuous absence of right angles, seem to ____ the radical designs that would later make her famous.
gre.clue: that would later make her famous

example: The young cricketer's fearless innings in school matches prefigured the attacking style that later made him a national star.

en: To speak or act evasively to avoid the truth
bn: সত্য এড়িয়ে যাওয়া; ঘুরিয়ে কথা বলা
hook: PREVARICATE: PRE-VARY the truth, twist it.
story: Prevaricate. Nayeem's mother asked him directly whether he had gone to his coaching class that day. He talked about the traffic, the heat, a friend who was sick, and how the teacher sometimes cancels classes. He never actually said yes or no. His mother sighed. He was prevaricating: speaking evasively to avoid the truth. Prevaricate comes from a Latin word for walking crookedly. Do not confuse it with procrastinate, which means to delay. Synonyms: equivocate, hedge, dodge.

gre.s: Pressed repeatedly about the missing funds, the treasurer continued to ____, offering vague answers that neither admitted nor denied any wrongdoing.
gre.clue: offering vague answers that neither admitted nor denied any wrongdoing

example: Asked by her mother where she had spent the afternoon, Tania prevaricated, mumbling something about a group study session.

en: Using too many words; tediously lengthy
hook: PROLIX: PRO at being LONG.
story: Prolix. The chief guest at the school prize-giving was supposed to speak for five minutes. He spoke for fifty. He repeated every point three times, told stories that led nowhere, and thanked each teacher by name, twice. The students fell asleep in rows. His speech was prolix: using too many words, tediously lengthy. Think: prolix speeches are prolonged. Synonyms: verbose, wordy, long-winded. Opposites: terse, concise, laconic.

gre.s: The editor urged the author to cut the manuscript in half, complaining that its ____ style buried every interesting idea under pages of needless detail.
gre.clue: buried every interesting idea under pages of needless detail

example: The ministry's prolix report ran to nine hundred pages, but its real findings could have fit on a single sheet.

en: To win or regain someone's favor by pleasing them
bn: তুষ্ট করা; সন্তুষ্ট করে প্রসন্ন করা
hook: PROPITIATE: make them PROPITIOUS (favorable) again.
story: Propitiate. Sabbir forgot his wife's birthday. The next morning he came home from the bazaar with her favourite roshogolla, a bunch of rajanigandha flowers, and an offer to cook dinner for a whole week. He was trying to propitiate her: to win back her favour by doing things that please her. In ancient times, people offered sacrifices to propitiate angry gods. The related adjective propitious means favourable. Synonyms: appease, placate, mollify.

gre.s: Hoping to ____ the furious shareholders, the board announced a generous special dividend and promised to replace the chief executive whose blunders had cost them so much.
gre.clue: announced a generous special dividend

example: To propitiate his angry wife after forgetting their anniversary, Habib cooked her favorite hilsa curry and bought jasmine garlands.

en: Complaining in a whining or irritable way
hook: QUERULOUS: always QUERYING and complaining.
story: Querulous. Chowdhury Saheb in flat 4B complains about everything. The lift is too slow, the guard too sleepy, the neighbours' children too loud, and the mangoes at the market too sour. Even on a perfect spring morning, he finds something to whine about in a thin, irritable voice. He is querulous: complaining in a whining, peevish way. The word comes from the Latin queri, to complain, the same root as quarrel. Synonyms: peevish, petulant, cantankerous.

gre.s: Age had made the once-genial professor ____: he now found fault with every seminar, every meal, and every student, and his letters to the dean consisted largely of complaints.
gre.clue: his letters to the dean consisted largely of complaints

example: The querulous passenger in the next seat complained about the food, the temperature and the movie throughout the long flight.

en: Known only to a few experts; hard to grasp
hook: RECONDITE: RE-CON-DITE, hidden like a secret condo deep in the hills.
story: Recondite. The visiting professor's lecture was on the grammar of an ancient Sanskrit dialect used by perhaps three monasteries a thousand years ago. Ten minutes in, the hall of two hundred students was lost. By the end, only two people understood him: his assistant and one very old librarian. The subject was recondite: obscure and difficult, known only to specialists. Recondite, arcane, abstruse, and esoteric are all heavy GRE words for hidden knowledge.

gre.s: Although the treatise addresses ____ questions of medieval theology, its author writes so clearly that even general readers can follow it.
gre.clue: even general readers can follow it

example: The old librarian could answer recondite questions about Mughal coinage that stumped even university professors.

en: Sleepy; drowsy; causing sleep
hook: SOMNOLENT: like inSOMNIA's opposite; full of sleep.
story: Somnolent. After the Eid lunch of rice, beef rezala, chicken roast, and three kinds of dessert, the whole family sank onto sofas and mattresses. Uncles snored. Aunties yawned mid-sentence. Even the cat dozed in a patch of sunlight. The afternoon passed in a warm, sleepy fog. Everyone was somnolent: drowsy and sleepy. Somnus means sleep, as in insomnia. A somnolent village dozes through the hot afternoon.

gre.s: The ____ atmosphere of the warm lecture hall, combined with the speaker's monotone, left half the audience struggling to stay awake.
gre.clue: left half the audience struggling to stay awake

example: On a hot afternoon the somnolent village seemed deserted, with only a few goats wandering past the closed shops.

en: To plead for something humbly and earnestly
hook: SUPPLICATE: on your knees, SUPPLYING prayers.
story: Supplicate. When the river swallowed his family's land, an old farmer travelled to the district office. He waited for hours, then knelt before the officer with folded hands and begged for a small plot of government land to rebuild his home. He was supplicating: asking or begging humbly. The noun is supplication, and a person who does it is a supplicant. Think: sub means under, and plicare means fold, so you fold yourself low. Synonyms: beseech, implore, entreat. Opposite: demand.

gre.s: Defeated and desperate, the rebel leaders could only ____ the emperor, kneeling humbly before the very throne they had once vowed to destroy.
gre.clue: kneeling humbly before the very throne

example: Standing before the visa officer, the elderly man could only supplicate for permission to attend his son's graduation abroad.

en: To weaken or ruin something so it no longer works properly
hook: VITIATE: makes it VICIOUS, corrupts it.
story: Vitiate. For six months, Ishita's research team ran an experiment on plant growth. Then they discovered that one thermometer had been broken from the start, showing the wrong temperature every single day. Every result became unreliable. Six months of work was useless. The faulty thermometer had vitiated the experiment: spoiled its quality and effectiveness. A single lie can vitiate a friendship; bias can vitiate research. Synonyms: impair, corrupt.

gre.s: A single undisclosed conflict of interest can ____ an otherwise rigorous study, rendering its conclusions suspect.
gre.clue: rendering its conclusions suspect

example: A missing signature on the final page vitiated the entire land contract, and the sale had to begin again.
